extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and scientific terminology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what constitutes a good definition in logic and science: distinguishes adequate vs imperfect definitions, technical (scientific) definitions, definitions vs descriptions, and the relation between definitions and postulates/existence claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate definition (declare the whole fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only adequate definition of a name is one which declares the facts, and the whole of the facts, which the name involves in its signification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strict/complete definition sets forth in words the constituent parts of the fact or phenomenon of which the connotation of the word is composed. This is the ideal of a scientific or full definition; all names (except names of elementary feelings) are in principle susceptible of such a definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions as guides to correct use (practical adequacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people seek in a definition nothing more than a guide to the correct use of the term — a protection against applying it inconsistently with custom and convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ordinary use an incomplete definition that indexes current usage may suffice even if it doesn't embrace the whole connotation. Such definitions are practically adequate for distinguishing presently known instances, but are liable to be overthrown by new discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential but incomplete definitions (part of connotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A connotative name may be defined by a part only of its connotation (essential but incomplete definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Man is a rational animal.' This may correctly indicate the present field of predication and usage even if it omits other connoted attributes. These are commonly used by logicians under the rule per genus et differentiam, but are vulnerable if new objects are discovered that share the stated attributes but lack the omitted ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental definitions / Descriptions (attributes not connoted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions that employ attributes not actually included in the connotation of the name are accidental definitions, or descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers have generally rejected such descriptions as genuine definitions. They arise from the practical willingness to accept any specification that discriminates the class from others. They may be raised to genuine definitions when, for a particular scientific or classificatory purpose, the term is given a special connotation (technical definition). Examples: 'Man is an animal who cooks his food', 'Man is a featherless biped.' The test of correctness is convertibility/coextensiveness with the name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convertibility / Co-extensiveness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct definition or description should be convertible with the name which it professes to define; that is, it should be exactly co-extensive with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defined phrase must be predicable of everything of which the name is predicable, and of nothing of which it is not predicable. Even a description (accidental definition) is acceptable only if it meets this co-extensiveness test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition should be drawn from the essence (not from accidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been a traditional rule that the definition must be drawn from the essence of the class; the attributes employed should really form part of the connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions formed in any degree from attributes not connoted by the name fail to satisfy this rule and are classed as descriptions rather than genuine definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per genus et differentiam rule and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Logicians often state that the definition of a species should be per genus et differentiam, but differentia is often taken as only one peculiar attribute rather than the whole set constitutive of the species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete definition would be per genus et differentias (plural) — include the genus and all the peculiar attributes. The doctrine that all definitions must be per genus et differentiam is not tenable for the highest genera (summum genus) and is problematic generally; definitions that merely give one differentia can be useful but are technically incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific (technical) definitions as classificatory tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific definitions commonly give a special connotation to a general name for the purposes of classification; their main object is to serve as landmarks of scientific classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because classifications change with advancing knowledge, scientific definitions are progressive and provisional. A technical definition may differ from ordinary meaning but preserves denotation while altering connotation to suit classificatory principles (e.g., Cuvier's definition of Man).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of names not definitions of things (avoid covert existence claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are properly of names only; what are called definitions of things covertly assert the existence of a thing with the specified attributes and thus include a postulate in addition to a nominal definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nominal definition explains the use of a term and is neither true nor false but only conformable or not to usage. A purported 'definition of a thing' contains, besides the nominal part, an implicit factual assertion (postulate) that instances exist. One must distinguish the two: conclusions about facts come from the postulate, not from the definition per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make implicit postulates explicit in demonstrative reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: In demonstrative sciences (e.g., geometry) what appear to be conclusions from definitions actually depend on tacit postulates (existence assumptions) involved in those definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Euclid: the 'definition' of a circle actually contains (1) an assumption that such a figure may exist (a postulate) and (2) the nominal definition. Demonstrations rest on the postulate; therefore one should state postulates explicitly rather than treating definitions as premises of demonstrative proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against deriving facts from mere definitions (non-entities example)
rubrics_metrics.description: If definitions were taken as factual premises, one could validly reason from true premises to false conclusions by defining non-existent entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: defining 'dragon' as 'a serpent breathing flame' is a correct nominal definition but does not imply existence. Using such definitions as factual premises yields absurd syllogisms. To avoid this error, distinguish between the nominal meaning and any assumed existence; substitute 'means' for 'is' to reveal nominal character of definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional nature of scientific definitions (adapt with knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions in the sciences are necessarily progressive and provisional because extension of knowledge may alter what particulars are included in the science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As scientific knowledge advances, attributes connoted by a term may recede or change (example: meanings of 'acid' and 'heat'). Accept that scientific definitions may change and be framed relative to current classificatory needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: When difficult/normative terms require deep inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Some questions of definition (e.g., 'What is justice?', 'What is rhetoric?') are difficult and may require deep investigation into the properties of the things named; sometimes the aim is to decide what the meaning should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For such philosophical or normative terms the task is not merely to record conventional usage but to propose a meaning suitable for practical or theoretical ends; this may entail detailed analysis of the things themselves and is a substantive intellectual task.
